title: Decode Hedger Adapter: acceptance latching, kernel-aware scoring, and staged failover
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Context: As we push to lower p95 token latency without sacrificing overall throughput, we need a runtime component that can perform low-cost 'hedged' decode attempts (fast path vs stable path) and decide early whether to commit to the fast output or gracefully switch to the stable decoder. This ticket implements the Decode Hedger Adapter: a kernel-aware acceptance latching layer that scores tentative decode outputs using lightweight metrics and orchestrates a staged failover policy.
goals: Provide a low-overhead acceptance metric that runs on prefill/prefix KV state + early tokens to decide accept/continue
Incorporate kernel selection signals (e.g., attention-window size, quantization mode, kernel fingerprint) into scoring so acceptance reflects runtime characteristics
Define a conservative staged failover: if acceptance is below threshold, smoothly route remaining tokens to stable decoder without user-facing anomalies
Ship telemetry and unit/e2e tests to validate acceptance calibration across model families and sequence distributions
non_goals: Replace full speculative decode system — this is an orthogonal hedging layer focused on fast verification of early output quality
Exhaustively tune thresholds for every single model in this ticket (follow-ups will handle broad calibration)
design_summary: The adapter sits between request routing and the decode execution pipeline. It accepts a tentative decode stream from a fast-path kernel (low-latency, aggressive quantization or shorter attention windows) and computes an acceptance_score using: a token-probability delta over the first N tokens, top-k entropy delta, prefix reconstruction error for deterministic prefixes, and a runtime penalty derived from kernel latency/variance fingerprint. If score >= accept_threshold, the adapter latches the fast stream and completes the response. If score < soft_threshold, the adapter initiates a staged failover: request a stable decode slot, bridge KV state if possible, and continue decoding on the stable path while retaining the option to discard fast-path partial tokens without returning inconsistent outputs to the client.
acceptance_metrics: acceptance_score: scalar in [0,1] computed as weighted sum of (prob_delta, entropy_delta, prefix_err, kernel_penalty)
early_reject_rate: fraction of fast-path attempts that trigger failover within first M tokens
latency_delta_committed: measured p50/p95 change when accepting vs failing
rollback_rate: fraction of in-flight fast outputs that are discarded post-failover
customer-visible_retries: count of client-observed reissues due to failover
fallback_playbook: Soft failover: when score < soft_threshold, enqueue request to stable pool and continue decoding tentatively; if stable becomes available before commit token, switch and discard tentative suffix
Hard failover: when score < hard_threshold or stable pool unavailable within deadline, trigger immediate switch to stable decoder and invalidate tentative tokens (return only after stable completes)
Graceful commit: if stable output closely matches tentative prefix (edit distance under threshold), merge to avoid user-visible duplication
Backpressure: if stable pool is saturated, fall back to conservative accept thresholds to avoid large rollback spikes
api_changes: Console: new per-route hedging toggle and threshold tuning controls
rollout_plan: Feature-flag gated rollout starting with internal canary (redwood-internal team) -> beta customers -> wide release
Phase 1: server-side only with default conservative thresholds and detailed telemetry collection
Phase 2: enable conservative hedging for selected high-frequency routes, collect calibration data
Phase 3: open threshold tuning to SRE and selected customers with runtime controls
Rollback: feature-flag off reverts to stable routing with no state migration required
test_plan: Unit tests for acceptance_score math and kernel_penalty mapping
Integration tests simulating kernel latency variance and quantized vs full kernels
E2E synthetic workloads (short prompts, long prompts, bursty traffic) measuring latency, rollback, and throughput
Chaos tests: induce stable pool saturation and GPU preemption to validate backpressure behavior
A/B benchmark against baseline on internal perf cluster; target: p95 latency reduction >= 10% on eligible routes with rollback_rate < 3%
tradeoffs_and_risks: Aggressive thresholds reduce p95 but increase rollback and wasted compute — must balance with cost budget
Kernel fingerprinting adds scheduling complexity and can bias selection towards specific hardware; mitigation: randomized probing
Hedged attempts consume transient capacity; if mismanaged, can worsen tail under high load — our staged failover and backpressure aim to limit this
Merging tentative and stable outputs is heuristic and may produce subtle content differences; we default to conservative merge criteria
implementation_notes: Map kernel_fingerprint -> latency_variance score via small offline microbenchmarks per kernel build
Implement acceptance scoring as a pluggable strategy so we can iterate (initial linear weights then move to a small learned logistic model)
KV transfer: prefer in-memory lightweight KV diffs; if incompatible, fall back to cold-start stable decode
Expose debug traces (non-PII) for each hedge attempt to the Console; add sampling to control storage
